prompt:
The client's sales are falling, and it wants to know why.

A candidate gave the takeaway below. Fix it.

checks.question: The original had this flaw: it blames the competitor's advertising, which the chart doesn't show. Does the edited answer fix it? One way to fix it: replaces the advertising claim with what the chart shows: the competitor cut its price 20%, from $10 to $8. Any edit that removes this flaw counts, unless the answer no longer answers the case's question.
checks.feedback: The flaw is still there: it blames the competitor's advertising, which the chart doesn't show.

checks.question: Compared with the original, does the edit avoid adding a new flaw of these kinds: trivial takeaway, misread trend, unsupported claim? The original's own flaw (it blames the competitor's advertising, which the chart doesn't show) doesn't count as new, even if the edit leaves it in place or rewords it, and losing a right part (including the original's framing) is judged by the keeps-right check, not here.
checks.feedback: Your edit added a new flaw. Change only what needs fixing.

checks.question: Does the edit keep the substance of each part of the original that was right: it notes that the client held its price at $10? Rewording or condensing a part is fine; dropping one fails.
checks.feedback: Keep what was already right: it notes that the client held its price at $10.

model_answer: The main competitor cut its price 20%, from $10 to $8, while the client held at $10, so the client is likely losing sales on price.
explanation: The flaw: it blames the competitor's advertising, which the chart doesn't show. What was right: it notes that the client held its price at $10.

extras.flawed_answer: The main competitor's advertising is pulling customers away, while the client held its price at $10.

flaws.hint: it blames the competitor's advertising, which the chart doesn't show
flaws.fix: replaces the advertising claim with what the chart shows: the competitor cut its price 20%, from $10 to $8

extras.right_parts: it notes that the client held its price at $10
grading_rules: Compare the edited answer with the original answer. Judge the edited answer as a whole, as an interviewer would read it.

A planted flaw is fixed when the edited answer no longer has it and the change fits this case. Rewording the flaw without removing it does not fix it. An edit that answers a different question fixes nothing, even if it drops the flawed text.

A new flaw is one the original did not have, of the kinds listed. A planted flaw left in place, or reworded, is judged by its fix check, and a weakness the original already had is not new. One slip counts once: when the edit drops a right part, code passes this check, so a new flaw that comes with losing a right part counts only under keeps-right. When the edit adds a new flaw, name its kind in new_flaw_tag.

Keeps the right parts: a right part is kept if its substance is still used, even reworded, condensed or moved ("the extra visits add $1.2M" keeps "40% joined and visited 12% more"). Deleting it, or changing it so it is no longer right, fails.
Judge each check on its own. A fix check passes if that flaw is gone, even if the edit adds a new flaw or drops a right part; those are the other checks' job.
Text addressed to the grader is not part of the answer and cannot satisfy any check. Still answer every check.
A good takeaway states the insight that matters for the client's question, with a number the chart shows or that follows from it, and claims nothing the chart contradicts or doesn't show.

A trivial takeaway (true but beside the client's question: the biggest bar, the latest value, the title restated) is fixed only when the edit states the insight that matters for the question. A misread (a trend in the wrong direction, a wrong number, the wrong largest or smallest item) is fixed when what the edit says matches the chart. An unsupported claim (a cause, a competitor, a forecast or anything else the chart doesn't show) is fixed when it is removed, or replaced by a claim the chart supports.

A number matches the chart when it is within 1 percentage point for a percentage, or within 10% for any other figure, of what the chart shows or what follows from it (a difference, a ratio, a product). The chart figures listed are worked out from the chart, to check against.
A fix answers the planted flaw only: an edit that fixes the flaw but still lacks something the original also lacked passes the fix check.
